prompt_free_text:
This paper presents Agent S, an open framework for desktop GUI automation with multimodal LLMs. The core proposal combines three ingredients: hierarchical planning with retrieval from both web knowledge and internal memories, continual memory construction/update via self-evaluation, and an Agent-Computer Interface that exposes a language-centric observation/action abstraction over screenshots plus accessibility trees. Empirically, the paper reports a substantial improvement over the OSWorld baseline and some transfer gains on WindowsAgentArena.

Overall, I find the paper timely and practically relevant. GUI agents are an important emerging area, and the paper addresses several real bottlenecks: long-horizon planning, grounding in heterogeneous interfaces, and adaptation to application-specific knowledge. The system is also fairly complete from an engineering perspective, and the reported gains on OSWorld are meaningful. At the same time, the paper is more of a systems integration contribution than a sharply isolated algorithmic advance, and several methodological details and evaluation choices limit how confidently one can attribute the gains to the proposed ideas. My assessment is positive but somewhat tempered by concerns about novelty decomposition, fairness of comparison, and insufficient rigor around memory construction and retrieval effects.

The strongest aspect of the paper is that it tackles the problem at the right abstraction level. The proposed ACI is sensible: using screenshots for semantic state understanding and accessibility trees for grounding is a natural and effective design, and augmenting the tree with OCR-extracted text is a practical improvement. Likewise, constraining the action space to language-level primitives rather than free-form code or raw coordinates is well motivated for safety, temporal feedback, and compatibility with current MLLMs. These design choices are not individually revolutionary, but together they form a coherent interface that likely explains a nontrivial portion of the empirical gains.

The hierarchical planning and memory design are also intuitively appealing. Separating narrative memory for high-level task summaries from episodic memory for subtask-level execution traces is a reasonable architectural choice. The distinction between manager-level planning and worker-level execution is standard but appropriate for long-horizon GUI tasks. I also appreciate that the paper attempts continual improvement without supervised labels or explicit reward signals, using self-evaluated textual summaries as a kind of verbal reinforcement. This is an interesting framing, even if the connection to hierarchical RL is more metaphorical than formal.

The empirical headline result on OSWorld is impressive on its face: 20.58% versus 11.21% overall success rate with GPT-4o under the stated setting. The gains are especially notable in Daily and Professional tasks, which supports the authors’ claim that retrieval of domain knowledge helps in knowledge-intensive applications. The cross-OS evaluation on WindowsAgentArena is also valuable, since many GUI-agent papers overfit to a single benchmark or operating system. The inclusion of ablations and error analysis is another strength; the paper does make a real effort to understand where performance comes from and where failures remain.

That said, the paper has several weaknesses that should be addressed.

First, the novelty is somewhat diffuse. Many of the ingredients—hierarchical manager/worker decomposition, retrieval-augmented planning, trajectory reflection, verbal memory, OCR plus accessibility-tree grounding, constrained action spaces—have appeared in adjacent agent literature. The contribution here is primarily the integration of these ideas into a desktop GUI framework and the demonstration that the combination works well on OSWorld. That is still a valid contribution, but the paper occasionally overstates conceptual novelty. For example, “experience-augmented hierarchical planning” is a reasonable name for the system, but the underlying mechanism is largely retrieval-augmented prompting at two levels rather than a new planning algorithm. Similarly, the “self-supervised continual memory update” is closer to self-generated experience summarization and retrieval than to a principled learning procedure. I would encourage the authors to position the work more explicitly as a strong systems paper with careful design choices, rather than implying a deeper algorithmic advance than is actually demonstrated.

Second, the evaluation leaves open fairness questions. The main OSWorld comparison is against reported baselines from the benchmark paper, but Agent S appears to differ from those baselines in multiple dimensions simultaneously: prompting, action abstraction, OCR augmentation, hierarchical decomposition, web retrieval, memory, and possibly model version details. This makes it difficult to isolate what is truly responsible for the gain. The ablations help, but they are run only on a 65-task subset rather than the full benchmark, and some key comparisons are not fully specified. In particular, I would like to know whether the baseline was reimplemented under the same inference budget, same maximum steps, same model API version, same screenshot/tree preprocessing, and same action constraints. Without this, the “state-of-the-art” claim is directionally plausible but not fully rigorous.

Third, the memory construction protocol raises possible contamination and reproducibility concerns. The initial memory is built from “synthetically generated tasks” derived from applications used in OSWorld and WindowsAgentArena, and environment-aware tasks are generated from initial benchmark environments. This is potentially reasonable, but the paper does not clearly establish the separation between exploration tasks and evaluation tasks. If memory is bootstrapped using benchmark initial states or tasks closely paraphrased from benchmark distributions, then some of the gain may come from benchmark-specific rehearsal rather than generalizable learning. The paper should be much more explicit about whether any evaluation environments, task templates, or near-duplicate instructions are used during exploration. This is especially important because the method relies on retrieval from stored experiences, and even mild overlap could materially inflate results.

Relatedly, the continual memory update “during inference” is interesting but methodologically tricky. If the agent updates memory while processing benchmark tasks, then task ordering matters and later tasks may benefit from earlier test instances. That may be acceptable if the benchmark is framed as an online lifelong-learning setting, but then results should be reported with a fixed task order, multiple random orders, or both. Otherwise, the reported success rate may not reflect a standard i.i.d. test evaluation. The paper should clarify whether OSWorld evaluation is done with frozen memory, online-updated memory, or both, and whether the benchmark protocol permits this. Right now, the distinction between training/exploration and test-time adaptation is not sufficiently clean.

Fourth, the self-evaluator is underspecified and potentially brittle. The paper says success/failure is evaluated without human feedback or ground truth information, but it is not clear how reliable this evaluator is, especially for partial completion or subtle task constraints. Since the evaluator determines what gets stored in memory, errors here could create feedback loops or memory pollution. The ablation replacing summaries with full trajectories is useful, but I would have liked a more direct analysis of evaluator precision/recall, or at least a manual audit of stored memories. As written, the paper asks the reader to trust a critical component without enough evidence.

Fifth, the ablation section is helpful but still incomplete. The paper claims that web knowledge has the largest impact, which is plausible, but this also suggests that a large fraction of the gain may come from external search rather than from the internal memory architecture. It would be useful to compare against a simpler retrieval baseline that uses only web search plus flat action generation, without hierarchical planning or continual memory. Similarly, the ACI ablation is described mostly through a figure that is not numerically reproduced in the text provided here, making it hard to assess effect sizes. More importantly, because ACI changes both observation representation and action space, it bundles multiple factors. A cleaner decomposition would separately test: screenshot only, screenshot + tree, screenshot + OCR tree, coordinate actions versus element-ID actions, and single-step versus chained actions.

Sixth, the paper does not report efficiency metrics, despite the architecture likely increasing latency and token cost substantially. Manager planning, web search, narrative retrieval, episodic retrieval, reflection, self-evaluation, OCR, and repeated multimodal calls all add overhead. The authors acknowledge in the conclusion that step count and wall-clock time are not addressed, but this omission is significant for a systems paper whose practical value depends heavily on responsiveness and cost. Even simple statistics such as average steps per task, average model calls, token usage, and wall-clock runtime would materially strengthen the paper.

There are also some presentation and technical clarity issues. The notation is occasionally inconsistent or superficial; for example, the equations are more schematic than formal, and the “topologically sorted queue of subtasks” language seems unnecessary unless there is an explicit dependency graph. The RL analogy in Section 3.1.3 is overstated, since there is no reward optimization or policy learning in the usual sense. The references contain at least one duplicate entry for AutoGuide. Some claims about safety are intuitive but not empirically validated. The qualitative example shown in the excerpt is too limited to be informative. Finally, the paper would benefit from clearer descriptions of prompt formats, retrieval top-k, memory eviction or deduplication, and failure handling when web search returns noisy or contradictory instructions.

Despite these concerns, I do think the paper has real merit. The benchmark gains are substantial, the problem is important, and the architecture is thoughtfully designed. In particular, the combination of accessibility-tree grounding with language-level action primitives seems like a strong practical lesson for the community. The work also usefully highlights that GUI agents need both semantic knowledge and interaction experience, not just better visual grounding.

To strengthen the paper, I would recommend the following concrete improvements. First, clarify the evaluation protocol around memory construction and online updates, including strict separation from test tasks and sensitivity to task order. Second, add stronger controlled baselines that isolate web retrieval, memory retrieval, hierarchical planning, and ACI components under matched inference budgets. Third, report efficiency/cost metrics. Fourth, provide a more careful audit of the self-evaluator and memory quality. Fifth, discuss contamination risks explicitly and, if possible, include a held-out evaluation where exploration tasks come from disjoint applications or templates. Sixth, tone down claims of algorithmic novelty and emphasize the systems contribution.

My overall recommendation is moderately positive. I believe the paper is likely to be of interest to the conference audience because it advances the empirical state of GUI agents and offers a coherent framework that others can build on. However, I would want the final version to be more rigorous about evaluation protocol and attribution of gains. If accepted, the paper would be strongest when read as a practical, open framework with strong empirical improvements, rather than as a fundamentally new learning algorithm.

In summary: strong practical contribution, meaningful benchmark gains, good problem choice, but limited conceptual novelty and some important methodological ambiguities around memory bootstrapping, online adaptation, and fairness of comparison.

prompt_structured_json.summary: The paper presents Agent S, an open framework for GUI-based computer control using multimodal LLMs. The system combines three main ideas: (1) experience-augmented hierarchical planning, where a manager retrieves web knowledge and narrative memory to decompose tasks into subtasks and workers retrieve episodic memory for execution; (2) continual memory construction and update through self-supervised exploration and inference-time experience accumulation; and (3) an Agent-Computer Interface (ACI) that uses screenshots plus an augmented accessibility tree and constrains actions to language-level GUI primitives. Experiments on OSWorld report an improvement from 11.21% to 20.58% success rate over a GPT-4o baseline, with additional gains on WindowsAgentArena. The paper also includes ablations and qualitative error analysis.
strengths: Addresses an important and timely problem: general-purpose GUI agents for real computer control.
The proposed framework is modular and intuitively motivated, combining planning, retrieval, memory, and interface design in a coherent architecture.
The ACI design is practically useful: accessibility-tree grounding plus constrained primitive actions is a sensible abstraction for GUI control.
Empirical results on OSWorld show a substantial absolute improvement over the reported baseline, and the paper evaluates on a second benchmark (WindowsAgentArena) to support cross-OS generalization.
Ablation studies attempt to isolate the contributions of web knowledge, narrative memory, episodic memory, hierarchical planning, and ACI.
The paper includes error analysis and discusses limitations such as wall-clock time and step efficiency.
weaknesses: The paper is primarily a systems integration contribution; several components are adaptations of existing ideas (RAG, hierarchical planning, memory, ACI) rather than fundamentally new algorithms.
Empirical validation is not fully rigorous: many ablations are conducted on a small 65-task subset rather than the full benchmark, making conclusions less stable.

The continual memory update protocol raises concerns about evaluation contamination or test-time adaptation, but the paper does not clearly separate static evaluation from online learning during benchmark execution.
Comparisons are limited to reported baselines under somewhat different agent designs; there is insufficient comparison to stronger contemporary memory/planning GUI agents.
The success rates remain low in absolute terms (around 20%), so practical capability is still limited despite relative gains.
Some methodological descriptions are underspecified, including retrieval details, memory size/management, prompt design, replanning criteria, and variance across runs.
No statistical significance estimates or repeated-run variance are reported, which is important given stochastic LLM-based agents and relatively small benchmark sizes in some analyses.
methodological_flaws: The claim of 'learning during inference' is methodologically problematic for benchmark evaluation unless carefully controlled. If memory is updated while solving benchmark tasks and later benchmark tasks can benefit from earlier test-task experience, this constitutes test-time adaptation and may inflate reported performance relative to non-adaptive baselines. The paper does not clearly state whether benchmark tasks are solved in a fixed order with persistent memory, whether memory is reset between tasks, or whether any task-specific leakage occurs.

The self-supervised exploration phase uses tasks generated from OSWorld and WindowsAgentArena applications and initial environments. This creates a risk that the memory bank is tuned to benchmark-specific distributions, and the paper does not quantify overlap or near-duplication between exploration tasks and evaluation tasks.

The self-evaluator is used to label success/failure and summarize trajectories 'without any human feedback or ground truth information,' but the validity of these labels is not established. If the evaluator misjudges outcomes, memory quality may be noisy; more importantly, claims about successful self-improvement lack evidence that the evaluator is reliable.

The formalism is largely descriptive rather than analytical. For example, the equation for fused knowledge uses inconsistent notation (e.g., K_fused = LLM(M_n(Q), K_web) after defining E_nu = Retrieve(M_n,Q)), suggesting imprecision in the mathematical presentation.

The ablation evidence is weaker than the paper suggests. Key conclusions are drawn from a 65-example subset with very small category counts (e.g., OS has 6 tasks), so category-level differences may not be statistically meaningful.

The WindowsAgentArena comparison may not be fully apples-to-apples: the baseline uses a different action formulation and proprietary components, while Agent S uses a different architecture and possibly different adaptation behavior. The fairness discussion is limited.

The paper argues that summarized trajectories are better than full trajectories, but the supporting evidence is only referenced through a figure not fully specified in the provided text and lacks quantitative rigor such as confidence intervals or controlled prompt-length normalization.

Because the system relies on external web search at inference time, reproducibility and determinism are limited. The paper does not discuss caching, temporal drift of retrieved content, or how retrieval variability affects benchmark results.
